citeinfo.title: Stream fish species abundance and associated physical habitat data in Catoctin Mountain Park (2015-2016)

descript.abstract: This Data Release provides records of fish species abundance collected during summer 2015 using single pass backpack electrofishing within sections of Owens Creek, Big Hunting Creek, and Blue Blazes Creek (a tributary to Big Hunting Creek) in Maryland (USA). We also provide water and air temperature data collected during at 30 minute increments summers of 2015 and 2016. Stream physical habitat data are also reported for fish sampling sites.
descript.purpose: Anticipating and mitigating the effects of climate change is a fundamental challenge for natural resource conservation. In this study, we respond to the research needs identified by Catoctin Mountain Park (CATO) personnel for coldwater stream conservation in the context of climate change. Native brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis) were identified as a high priority for research due to their natural and cultural importance and dependence on coldwater habitats which are threatened by climate change.

procstep.procdesc:
There was data editing involved in the creation of the "CATO_WaterAir_HourlyTemperature_2015-2016_DataRelease" and the editing process is described below.
Water temperature data downloaded from each site gage were combined and quality checked in program R. At some sites, stream drying occurred over some time periods and in those cases, measurements are not representative of water temperature. To identify drying periods, temperature data for each site was graphed over the period of record and qualitative assessments of these graphs were used to parse out dry periods (inferred from spikes or outliers in temperature measurements). Water temperature measurements at dates where sites were deemed "dry" or "likely dry" from these assessments were removed from the final data set prior to analysis and publication. We removed data from two water temperature sites entirely (BA03 and BA04) that apparently dried during summer months. Following editing, water temperature data from all gages for the period of record were merged to form the ""CATO_WaterAir_HourlyTemperature_2015-2016_DataRelease"" entity.
Air temperature data downloaded from each site gage were combined and quality checked in program R. We removed short-term spikes from air temperature gages associated with direct solar incidence. At some sites, air temperature data exhibited steep spikes in air temperature at specific mid-day time periods due to direct exposure to sunlight that caused rapid heating. In these cases, we performed a "spike" correction to air temperature data whereby hourly measurements that were >3 degrees (C) different from the previous hourly measurement were replaced with the average of the temperature measurement from the hour before and the hour after. Following editing, air temperature data from all gages for the period of record were merged to form the ""CATO_WaterAir_HourlyTemperature_2015-2016_DataRelease"" entity.

method.methdesc:
We deployed 64 ONSET ProV2 water temperature gages in Owens Creek (n=36), upper Big Hunting Creek (n=21), and Blue Blazes Creek (n=7) to collect data at stations located approximately 200 m apart (Figure 2) during summer months of 2015 and 2016. Prior research has demonstrated the necessity of stream temperature data at this spatial scale for forecasting stream thermal responses to climate change in Appalachia (Snyder et al. 2015; Johnson et al. 2017). We programmed gages to collect temperature data every 30 minutes during the sampling period. Gages were placed in drilled PVC cases and anchored to the substrate with rebar. We also used the same type of gage to collect air temperature data at a subset of sites (n=6). We calibrated all gages prior to deployment in a water bath of known temperature. Gages were removed after the study completed.
Fish sampling was conducted during baseflow conditions (i.e., avoiding storm events). We used a Smith-Root LR-45 backpack electrofisher (typically set to 300V, 60Hz, and 20% duty cycle) and dipnets to collect stunned fish. All fish were identified to species and tallied. Length and weight data were collected for individual trout specimens. Following sampling, fish were released into the sampling reach (with some exceptions for sculpin Dermocystidium sampling in Blue Blazes Creek). We did not observe fish mortalities as a result of electrofishing.
Immediately following electroshocking, a habitat crew collected data in the reach. A 5m rope was extended from the downstream blocknet straight up the middle of the stream. At each 5m interval, water depth, mesohabitat, and substrate were recorded at 3 places along a transect perpendicular to flow. Wetted width was measured, temperature was recorded, and single or split channel was noted for the transect. For split channels, wetted width was measured in each channel and added together for the total. In the case of two channels, two depth-meso-substrate measurements were taken in the channel with most flow and one in the other channel. We also noted if a temperature logger was located near each transect. A total tally of two classes of large woody debris was recorded for the 100m reach. Data was collected on paper forms or in a field notebook when forms were not available.
